questions.question_text: You are reviewing cases in an addiction clinic, and note in the file that your next patient has previously experienced 'formication'. What kind of hallucination is formication?
questions.explanation: A haptic hallucination is a hallucination of touch. Formication is a form of tactile (or haptic) hallucination in which there is the sensation of numerous insects crawling over the surface of the body. This is not uncommon in acute organic states, including alcohol or drug withdrawal, particularly from cocaine. It is a form of superficial hallucination. The other forms of hallucinations listed above are also superficial hallucinations. Visceral hallucination is false perceptions of internal organs such as throbbing. Kinaesthetic hallucination is false perceptions of joint muscles (e.g. twisting or vibrating). Hygric hallucination is false perception of fluid. Thermal hallucination is false perception of hot and cold.

questions.question_text: Donna and Malcom have had concerns about their son, Stuart, who is 6 years old and doesn't seem to be developing social skills in the same way as many of his peers. He dislikes being in groups, tends to spend a lot of time alone, immersed in quite a narrow repertoire of interests. If his usual routine is disrupted he can become very upset and difficult to comfort. Donna and Malcom have been searching the internet, reading about Autistic Spectrum Disorder, and how it is categorised in diagnostic manuals. Which one of the following statements is true regarding diagnostic categorisation in ICD and DSM?

options.text: DSM 5 categorises Autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) under neurodevelopmental disorders
DSM 5 has a category for pervasive developmental disorder
DSM 5 includes language development as a core feature of Autistic spectrum disorder (ASD)
ICD-11 has a category for pervasive developmental disorder
DSM 5 has a category for overactive disorder associated with mental retardation

correct_answer.text: DSM 5 categorises Autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) under neurodevelopmental disorders

correct_answers.text: DSM 5 categorises Autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) under neurodevelopmental disorders

questions.explanation: DSM 5 describes three 'severity levels' associated with the diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder. Diagnostic criteria include persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts; and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, with symptoms present in the early developmental period and causing impairment in functioning. For persistent difficulties in the social use of verbal and nonverbal communication, a DSM 5 diagnosis of Social Communication Disorder should be considered.

questions.question_text: John Tulley is known to have epilepsy. On Saturday he attended a live rock concert with some of his friends. He had one pint of beer to drink. At one point during the concert, he fell to the ground and began to shake. The appearance was in keeping with a generalised epileptic seizure. Once the shaking had stopped, John began to regain consciousness. He sat up and was moving his arms, seemingly without purpose. His speech was not coherent, and he pursed his lips repeatedly. This lasted for approximately 10 minutes. John didn't recall this having happened when he was asked about it. What is the term used for this phase?
questions.explanation: The term 'twilight state' describes conditions in which there is a restriction of the morbidly changed consciousness, a break in the continuity of consciousness, and relatively well-ordered behaviour. If one keeps strictly to these criteria, then the commonest twilight state is the result of epilepsy.

questions.question_text: Hana Haq is a 42-year-old woman, who has presented to her GP with features of depression following the loss of her mother from cancer. For the past month she has been waking up a few hours earlier than usual. Her appetite has decreased (she has lost half a stone in weight) and she feels generally demotivated and hopeless, taking little pleasure from her usual activities. The GP fills out the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D) in order to ascertain the severity of her depression. Which of the following statements is true of the HAM-D?

options.text: It has a section on weight loss
It is scored out of a total of 8 points
It excludes behavioural aspects of depression
It does not allow for estimation of severity

correct_answer.text: It has a section on weight loss

correct_answers.text: It has a section on weight loss

questions.explanation: The Hamilton Depression Rating Scale is a widely used scale for measuring depression, consisting of a list of 17 items, designed to be rated by a clinician on three-point and five-point scales. The symptoms are: depressed mood, guilt feelings, suicide, insomnia (initial or early), insomnia (middle), insomnia (terminal or late), disturbed work and activities, psychomotor retardation, psychomotor agitation, anxiety (psychological), anxiety (somatic), gastrointestinal symptoms, somatic symptoms, sexual dysfunction or menstrual disturbance, hypochondriasis, weight loss, and lack of insight. The maximum score is 52, and the following interpretation of scores is often used: 10-13 mild depression; 14-17 moderate depression; 18-30 marked depression; >30 severe depression.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about the diagnosis of delusional disorder?

options.text: General speech and behaviour are not typically affected
ICD-11 requires the symptoms to be present for 6 months
ICD-11 classifies delusional disorder under neurotic disorders
Delusions typically vary from day to day
Delusional disorder is associated with mood symptoms

correct_answer.text: General speech and behaviour are not typically affected

correct_answers.text: General speech and behaviour are not typically affected

questions.explanation: Delusional disorder is characterised by the development of a delusion or set of related delusions, typically persisting for at least 3 months and often much longer, in the absence of a depressive, manic, or mixed mood episode. The delusions are variable in content across individuals, but typically stable within individuals, although they may evolve over time. Other characteristic symptoms of schizophrenia (i.e. clear and persistent hallucinations, negative symptoms, disorganised thinking, or experiences of influence, passivity, or control) are not present, although various forms of perceptual disturbances (e.g. hallucinations, illusions, misidentification of persons) thematically related to the delusion are still consistent with the diagnosis. Apart from actions and attitudes directly related to the delusion or delusional system, affect, speech, and behaviour are typically unaffected.

questions.question_text: Bobby is a 22-year-old man, who has been brought to A&E with his mother, following their involvement in a serious road traffic accident. His mother was very badly injured, and sadly, whilst in the A&E, she dies. You are asked to go and speak to him. You find him to be in intense emotional distress: crying, sometimes sobbing, and unable to find coherent words to express himself. He says that it all feels unreal, and it's as if he's floating outside his body. What term is most appropriate to describe what is happening to Bobby?
questions.explanation: Acute stress reaction refers to the development of transient emotional, somatic, cognitive, or behavioural symptoms as a result of exposure to an event or situation (either short- or long-lasting) of an extremely threatening or horrific nature. Symptoms may include autonomic signs of anxiety (e.g. tachycardia, sweating, flushing), being in a daze, confusion, sadness, anxiety, anger, despair, overactivity, inactivity, social withdrawal, or stupor. The response to the stressor is considered to be normal given the severity of the stressor (it is not considered a disorder in ICD-11), and usually begins to subside within a few days after the event or following removal from the threatening situation.

questions.question_text: Priscilla is a 19-year-old woman whose mother has insisted she come to see you because she is worried about how thin she is. Priscilla tells you that she doesn't believe herself to be too thin. In fact, she thinks that she could do with losing more weight. She exercises four times a day, restricts her intake to a couple of apples and half a piece of toast a day. She has stopped menstruating. Her BMI is 15, and her T3 levels are normal. What's the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa is characterised by significantly low body weight for the individual's height, age, and developmental stage that is not due to another health condition or the unavailability of food. A commonly used threshold is body mass index (BMI) less than 18.5 in adults. Low body weight is accompanied by a persistent pattern of behaviours to prevent restoration of normal weight, which may include behaviours aimed at reducing energy intake (restricted eating) purging behaviours (e.g. self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives), and behaviours aimed at increasing energy expenditure (e.g. excessive exercise), typically associated with a fear of weight gain. Low body weight or shape is central to the person's self-evaluation or is inaccurately perceived to be normal or even excessive. T3 levels are not part of the diagnostic criteria; commonly, T3 levels in anorexia nervosa are low, but not in every case.

questions.question_text: What is least likely with regard to sleep terrors?

options.text: Occurs in deep slow wave sleep
Often seen during early nocturnal sleep
Increased autonomic arousal is noted during the episode

questions.explanation: Sleep terrors are recurrent episodes of abrupt awakening from sleep characterised by a panicky scream, with intense fear and autonomic arousal. The individual usually has no recall of the details of the event and is unresponsive to stimuli (e.g. conversation) during the episode. They occur during the first third of the night, during slow-wave stage 3 of NREM sleep. Autonomic hyperactivity is manifested by tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis, flushed face, dilated pupils, agitation, tremulousness, and increased muscle tone. A typical episode lasts no more than a few minutes, but may be protracted, lasting up to an hour.

questions.question_text: Which of the following clinical features suggests a diagnosis of social phobia rather than agoraphobia?

options.text: Having a fear of getting into situations of no escape
Having a fear of being under continuous scrutiny from others
Avoiding the use of public transport

correct_answer.text: Having a fear of being under continuous scrutiny from others

correct_answers.text: Having a fear of being under continuous scrutiny from others

questions.explanation: Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) is characterised by marked and excessive fear or anxiety that consistently occurs in one or more social situations such as social interactions, doing something while feeling observed, or performing in front of others. The individual is concerned that they will act in a way, or show anxiety symptoms, that will be negatively evaluated by others. Relevant social situations are consistently avoided or else endured with intense fear or anxiety. Somatic symptoms include blushing, trembling, dry mouth, and perspiration. There is a high level of comorbidity with substance misuse. Both social phobia and agoraphobia can present with house-bound behaviour and avoiding public places. But in patients with social phobia the underlying fear is that of embarrassing oneself by 'doing something stupid' while others are watching them.

questions.question_text: Marie presents with a first episode of depression. She is started on an SSRI. Seven days later, she is found to be overactive, easily distractible, irritable and sleepless, which lasts for about 5 days. The symptoms resolve when the SSRI was stopped. Most appropriate diagnosis among the following list is
questions.explanation: With respect to bipolar disorders, both DSM-5 and ICD-11 exclude syndromes caused by the effects of a substance or medication, another medical condition (tumour, etc.), but now allow for the diagnosis of a manic or hypomanic episode if the full syndrome persists after antidepressant treatment (e.g. medication, ECT, light therapy) is discontinued and its direct effects have ceased or receded.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old woman is referred by her GP. She states that her eyes are set wide apart and people call her 'fish-face'. She spends hours in front of the mirror examining her eyes. She has seen surgeons twice to get plastic surgery done to her eye folds. However there is no obvious deformity. The most appropriate diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Body dysmorphic disorder is characterised by a persistent preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in appearance that are either unnoticeable or only slightly noticeable to others. Individuals experience excessive self-consciousness, often with ideas of reference (i.e., the conviction that people are taking notice, judging, or talking about the perceived defect or flaw). In response to their preoccupation, individuals engage in repetitive and excessive behaviours that include repeated examination of the appearance or severity of the perceived defect or flaw, excessive attempts to camouflage or alter the perceived defect, or marked avoidance of social situations or triggers that increase distress about the perceived defect or flaw.

questions.question_text: A 36-year-old woman complains of severe tiredness not relieved by rest for over 6 months and is unable to work. There is no identifiable organic pathology and she denies any pain in her body. The most appropriate diagnosis is
questions.explanation: CDC criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome: Main criteria – persistent or relapsing fatigue of 6 months duration or more; fatigue not explained by any concurrent somatic or psychiatric condition; fatigue is new or has a defined onset; fatigue is not due to ongoing exertion; fatigue is not relieved by rest. Additional criteria (at least 4): impaired memory and/or concentration; sore throat; tender lymph nodes; muscle pain; multi-joint pain; new headaches; unrefreshing sleep; post-exertional malaise. Exclusion criteria include medical conditions explaining fatigue, significant psychiatric disorders within 2 years before onset, severe obesity (BMI >45), or unexplained exam/lab abnormalities suggesting exclusionary conditions.

questions.question_text: Unstable affect and impulsive behaviour is characterised by which of the following personality disorders, according to DSM-5 Criteria?
questions.explanation: DSM-5 uses three broad clusters to organise the categories of personality disorders: Cluster A (odd/eccentric): paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal; Cluster B (emotional/dramatic): antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic, borderline; Cluster C (fearful/anxious): avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old lady has a history of olfactory hallucinations along with flushing. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Preictal events (auras) in complex partial seizures include autonomic sensations (e.g., fullness in the stomach, blushing, and changes in respiration); cognitive sensations (e.g., déjà vu, jamais vu, forced thinking, dreamy states); affective states (e.g., fear, panic, depression, elation); and classically, automatisms (e.g., lip smacking, rubbing, chewing). Wilder Penfield reported that fewer than 1% of patients with partial-onset seizures experienced olfactory symptoms. The majority of patients with epilepsy and olfactory auras will have clear complex partial or secondary generalized seizures in addition to their sensory symptoms although these episodes may occur at separate times.

questions.question_text: A woman presents to A&E with the following features: weight loss, fatigue, hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) is characterised by chronic glucocorticoid and/or mineralocorticoid deficiency due to failure of the adrenal cortex. It should be suspected in all acutely or chronically ill patients with general fatigue or severe weakness and unexplained dehydration, hypotension, weight loss, fever, abdominal pain and hyperpigmentation. Key lab characteristics include hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and (especially in children) hypoglycemia. Psychiatric symptoms include apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, and depressed mood. It may be misdiagnosed as major depressive disorder. Anorexia is common in both depression and Addison's, but the presence of nausea, vomiting and hyperpigmentation may suggest Addison's disease. The most common symptoms of Addison's are fatigue, muscle weakness, fever, weight loss, darkening (hyperpigmentation) of the skin, including areas not exposed to the sun, and orthostatic hypotension.

questions.question_text: Mr. Welton's memory is being tested. He has been given a list of items to study. Once he has finished studying the items he is given another list to study, before being asked to recall as many items as he can from the first list, in any order. What memory test does this allude to?
questions.explanation: Free recall is the retrieval of information from memory without the help of cues, and hence often contrasted with cued recall. This term is also used for retrieval of a number of items of information in any order, in contradistinction to serial recall. In this case, the free recall is also delayed.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y has a history of alcohol dependence. He is admitted to a medical ward as he developed memory difficulties following Wernicke's encephalopathy. The bedside test most likely to be impaired is
questions.explanation: Korsakoff syndrome is characterised by the absence or significant impairment in the ability to lay down new memories, together with a variable length of retrograde amnesia. Working memory (e.g. ability to remember a sequence of numbers) is unimpaired, as is procedural and 'emotional' memory. Korsakoff syndrome is a preventable memory disorder that usually emerges (although not always) in the aftermath of an episode of Wernicke's encephalopathy. Episodic memory is severely affected in the Korsakoff syndrome, and the learning of new semantic memories is variably affected. 'Implicit' aspects of memory are preserved.

questions.question_text: On ocular examination of a 74-year-old patient, constriction of pupils is noted on looking at near objects but no reaction to light. This is called
questions.explanation: An Argyll-Robertson pupil (ARP) is a pupil of the eye that manifests accommodation by constricting when watching a finger that is brought close to the face but does not respond to light by constricting, a neurological sign of damage to the midbrain relays of the oculomotor nerve. In ARP, the pupils are bilaterally small and reduce in size when the patient focuses on a near object (i.e. Accommodation Reflexes Present) but do not constrict when exposed to bright light (i.e. pupillary reflexes absent). They are seen in patients with neurosyphilis (hence the name 'Prostitute's Pupil') and diabetic neuropathy.

questions.question_text: You note tonic spasm in a woman who cannot resist closing her right eye while talking to you. She is able to carry out most of her daily activities including watching television normally. This is best described as
questions.explanation: Blepharospasm is a movement disorder characterised by hyperactivity of the orbicularis oculi and of other muscles around the eyes. In addition to motor features, blepharospasm patients may also have nonmotor manifestations, including psychiatric, mild cognitive, and sensory disturbances. The various motor and nonmotor symptoms are not present in all patients, suggesting that blepharospasm is phenomenologically a heterogeneous condition.

questions.question_text: A patient with schizophrenia is observed in the waiting room with various semi-purposive movements, with an inability to change the movements at will or make them goal-directed. This is best described as
questions.explanation: Catatonia is a psychomotor syndrome that has been reported to occur in more than 10% of patients with acute psychiatric illnesses. Two subtypes of the syndrome have been identified. Catatonia of the retarded type is characterised by immobility, mutism, staring, rigidity, and a host of other clinical signs. Excited catatonia is a less common presentation in which patients develop prolonged periods of psychomotor agitation. The psychomotor agitation of excited catatonia can appear similar to akathisia.

questions.question_text: The following is the most common obsession in OCD:
questions.explanation: The most common pattern in OCD is an obsession of contamination, followed by washing or accompanied by compulsive avoidance of the presumably contaminated object. The feared object is often hard to avoid (e.g. faeces, urine, dust, or germs). Patients with contamination obsessions usually believe that the contamination is spread from object to object or person to person by the slightest contact.

questions.question_text: When asked what he did for a living, a patient stated that he worked at a shop selling clothes. He went on to say 'I don't like the messages on t-shirts. I wish I was a sailor'. He is exhibiting
questions.explanation: Circumstantial thinking is a disorder of the form of thought where irrelevant details and digressions overwhelm the direction of the thought process. This abnormality may be reflected in the resultant speech and can be seen in a number of conditions including mania and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (not OCD).

questions.question_text: A 44 year old woman is terrified of heights. She develops a sense of vertigo even at 1st or 2nd floor of a building and avoids high rise buildings at all cost. The company she is working for undergoes relocation and she is required now to work at 15th floor of a building in central London. Which of the following is the best treatment option for her?
questions.explanation: Simple phobias such as acrophobia can be treated with the behavioural technique of systematic desensitisation. Systematic desensitisation is based on the behavioural principle of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). It involves three steps: relaxation training, constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and desensitisation of the stimulus. The patient is exposed to a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking situations in stepwise fashion while being taught to practice the relaxation techniques.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man who works for the state as a highway and bridge designer becomes extremely anxious when he has to drive across any bridge. Which technique can best help him?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation can reduce anxiety in a situation by identifying a hierarchy of situations that produce anxiety from low to high. For example, the bridge designer can be taught progressive muscle relaxation until he is as relaxed as possible, at which point he will begin by driving across the shortest or least anxiety-producing bridge (in vivo exposure). As he successfully experiences crossing the lowest anxiety-producing bridge, he can proceed up the hierarchy of bridges until he masters crossing the most anxiety-producing bridge. Systematic desensitisation is based on the behavioural principle of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). It involves three steps: relaxation training, constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and desensitisation of the stimulus. The patient is exposed to a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking situations in stepwise fashion while being taught to practice the relaxation techniques.

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist shows several pictures to encourage her patient to narrate imaginative stories and descriptions. On the basis of the responses, she makes an assessment of the patient's personality. Which of the following best describes this test?
questions.explanation: The thematic apperception test is a projective personality test. It consists of a series of 10 black-and-white pictures that depict individuals of both sexes and of different age groups, who are involved in a variety of different activities. The stories that the patient makes up concerning the pictures, according to the projective hypothesis, reflect the patient's own needs, thoughts, feelings, stresses, wishes, desires, and views of the future.

questions.question_text: According to Eysenck's three-factor theory which of the following is a feature of an extravert person?

options.text: They have a less reactive reticular activating system
They have an overactive reticular activating system
They have a high autonomic lability

correct_answer.text: They have a less reactive reticular activating system

correct_answers.text: They have a less reactive reticular activating system

questions.explanation: Eysenck believed that differences in extraversion were due to physiological differences in brain systems that caused some people to be more easily aroused than others. Specifically, he proposed that the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) regulated arousal. People differ in the sensitivity of this system, which causes them to respond differently to their environment. A moderately stimulating environment might cause people with a very sensitive ARAS to feel overstimulated and retreat (i.e., to behave like introverts), but people with a less sensitive ARAS to feel under-stimulated and seek out additional stimulation (i.e., to behave like extraverts).

questions.question_text: Recalling an address with three items tests which one of the following?
questions.explanation: Verbal memory refers to the memory of words and other abstractions involving language.

questions.question_text: A 39-year-old man can be tested for current IQ using
questions.explanation: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scales are for people aged 16 and over.

questions.question_text: Iconic memory lasts for
questions.explanation: Iconic memory holds stimuli for up to a second. As a consequence, the flow of visual information seems smooth and continuous. The memory traces of auditory stimuli can last for several seconds, many times longer than the traces of visual stimuli. Iconic memory (or iconic store) is one of the sensory registers, allowing a visual image to persist for about half a second (depending on brightness) after a stimulus has ceased. It enables television, which presents 25 still images per second, each given twice to raise the flicker rate to 50 per second, to convey the illusion of a single continuous image which can be perceived as a moving image.

questions.question_text: A forensic investigator tries to reconstruct the crime scene and encourages the witnesses to visit the scene of crime to aid this process. Which recall phenomenon is being utilized by this investigator?
questions.explanation: Context-dependent memory is a form of state-dependent memory associated with the context in which information is learned and recalled. In a frequently-cited British experiment on context-dependent memory, lists of words that were learned by divers while they were underwater were best recalled when they were again underwater, and conversely words learned on land were best recalled on land.

questions.question_text: John loves to gamble using slot machines in the casinos. The reinforcement achieved using slot machines is a type of
questions.explanation: In operant conditioning, a variable-ratio schedule is one in which a reward is delivered after the organism has made a random number of responses, and is then rewarded after a further random number of responses, and so on. Ratio schedules, especially variable ratio schedules, can generate high rates of behaviour, as seen in the behaviour directed at a casino slot machine.

questions.question_text: The Thematic Apperception Test is a projective test of
questions.explanation: The thematic apperception test is a projective personality test. It consists of a series of 10 black-and-white pictures that depict individuals of both sexes and of different age groups, who are involved in a variety of different activities. The stories that the patient makes up concerning the pictures, according to the projective hypothesis, reflect the patient's own needs, thoughts, feelings, stresses, wishes, desires, and views of the future.

questions.question_text: A gentleman gets his pay cheque on the first day of every month. His salary provides which one of the following types of reinforcement?
questions.explanation: A fixed-interval schedule is when behaviour is rewarded after a set amount of time. This type of schedule exists in payment systems when someone is paid hourly, weekly or monthly: no matter how much work that person does in one hour, week or month (behaviour), they will be paid the same amount (reinforcement). In operant conditioning, a fixed-interval schedule is a simple reinforcement schedule in which reward follows the first response that the organism makes after a predetermined time interval, and then the first response that it makes after the same interval, and so on.

questions.question_text: Dr. Lepage is a GP who gets extra payments for every additional hour of clinical work that he undertakes. This reinforcement schedule is an example of
questions.explanation: With a fixed-ratio schedule, there are a set number of responses that must occur before the behaviour is rewarded. In this example, the doctor earns extra money for every extra hour of clinic he does (interval is fixed). Fixed ratios are better suited to optimize the quantity of output, whereas a fixed interval can lead to a higher quality of output. In operant conditioning, a fixed-interval schedule is a simple reinforcement schedule in which reward follows the first response that the organism makes after a predetermined time interval, and then the first response that it makes after the same interval, and so on.

questions.question_text: After a consultation with a GP, one of your patients was able to recall verbatim the opening statement asked by the GP. This is described as
questions.explanation: In serial learning, the primacy effect is a tendency for the items near the beginning of the series to be better recalled than those near the middle.

questions.question_text: William Tuke's approach to the treatment of insanity was called
questions.explanation: William Tuke was a 19th century reformist and philanthropist notable for his work in mental health. He pioneered the use of moral treatment, a humane method of treating mental illness. This focused on allowing patients to live in a community, partake in daily activities, and not be subjected to the brutality of the commonplace asylum.

questions.question_text: The term stigma was first popularised by
questions.explanation: Stigma is a mark of disgrace associated with a person, a personal quality, or a personal circumstance. The term was introduced into the social sciences by sociologist Erving Goffman in a book entitled 'Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity'.

questions.question_text: A psychosomatic family process has been described in association with eating disorders. The features of such a psychosomatic family includes
questions.explanation: Minuchin and colleagues defined predominant characteristics of families with an anorectic adolescent (so-called 'psychosomatic families'), including enmeshment, rigidity, insufficient conflict resolution skills, and overprotectiveness.

questions.question_text: Select the correct statement regarding schizophrenia in African-Caribbean population

options.text: Second generation African-Caribbeans with schizophrenia are more likely to develop negative symptoms
An increased rate of schizophrenia is not found in Jamaica, the country of origin for most African-Caribbeans in the UK.
The rate of prescription of depot medications for second generation African-Caribbeans in the UK are the same as that of Caucasian subjects
Second generation African-Caribbeans with Schizophrenia are more likely to have a continuous unremitting illness
The first admission rates for second generation African-Caribbeans in the UK are the same as that of Caucasian subjects

correct_answer.text: An increased rate of schizophrenia is not found in Jamaica, the country of origin for most African-Caribbeans in the UK.

correct_answers.text: An increased rate of schizophrenia is not found in Jamaica, the country of origin for most African-Caribbeans in the UK.

questions.explanation: First and second generation Afro-Caribbean migrants to the UK have increased rates of psychotic illnesses. The rates of schizophrenia in Caribbean countries are no higher than the incidence rates for the native White people in Britain, suggesting genetic predisposition alone cannot account for the high reported rates in the UK.

questions.question_text: The Tarasoff case was related to
questions.explanation: In the Tarasoff case, the Supreme Court decided that physicians and therapists have a duty to warn third parties of threatened danger arising from a patient's violent intentions, stating 'protective privilege ends where public peril begins.' This ruling relates to confidentiality.

questions.question_text: The double-bind theory in schizophrenia refers to

options.text: Giving contradictory messages to a child
Parents downgrading the roles of each other
One parent assumes a dominant and the other a submissive role
Lack of motivation to remain abstinent from cocaine use
Migration being a precipitant for psychosis

correct_answer.text: Giving contradictory messages to a child

correct_answers.text: Giving contradictory messages to a child

questions.explanation: Gregory Bateson and Donald Jackson formulated the double bind concept to describe a hypothetical family in which children receive conflicting parental messages about their behaviour, attitude, and feelings. According to Bateson's hypothesis, children withdraw into a psychotic state to escape the unsolvable confusion of the double bind.

questions.question_text: The average age of the earliest retrieved memory is
questions.explanation: The average age of the earliest retrieved memory is 3.5 years. Infantile or childhood amnesia refers to the inability of adults to remember episodic experiences that occurred during the first few years of life (generally 0–3 years) and the tendency to have sparse recollection of events before age 10. This cannot be explained simply by the passage of time or difference in encoding ability, suggesting developmental differences in hippocampus-dependent memory processing.

questions.question_text: Infants exhibit the capacity for colour vision and accommodation at the age of
questions.explanation: At birth, infants can track and scan objects, discriminate levels of brightness, fix objects at about 20 cm, and perform figure-ground discrimination, though visual acuity is slightly impaired. At 1 month they differentiate faces; at 2 months they possess depth perception and prefer three-dimensional representations of a face; at 4 months colour vision and accommodation develop; and at 6 months accurate acuity (6:6) is achieved.

questions.question_text: In a Strange Situation experiment, a 2-year-old girl continues to play without getting disturbed when her mother leaves the room and does not show any response when she comes back. What type of attachment is seen here?
questions.explanation: Anxious avoidant attachment is characterized by indifference towards the caregiver’s departure and return. In Mary Ainsworth’s Strange Situation, children with insecure-avoidant attachment seem unconcerned at separation or reunion and can be comforted by a stranger as easily as by the parent. It is associated with unresponsive parenting.

questions.question_text: A boy can identify that two balls are of the same size even though they appear to be of different sizes due to a distance illusion. This corresponds to which stage of Piaget's cognitive development?
questions.explanation: According to Piaget, the stage of concrete operations (ages 7–11 years) is when children can perform operations on concrete objects and understand conservation—that although the shape of objects may change, they maintain characteristics such as size and number. Identifying that two balls remain the same size despite a distance illusion is an example of conservation.

questions.question_text: You are a CT1 psychiatric trainee. One of your patients on the ward who is a 62-year-old man has an acute onset chest pain and sweating. Accompanying ECG showed ST elevation in leads V1-4. What is the abnormality?
questions.explanation: ST elevation and/or Q waves in leads V1–V4 is suggestive of an anterior wall myocardial infarction (MI).

questions.question_text: Which of the following defence mechanisms involves realistic planning for future discomfort?
questions.explanation: Anticipation is a mature defence mechanism involving realistic planning for future inner discomfort, implying concerned planning, worrying, and anticipation of possible outcomes.

questions.question_text: The expression of ideas, thoughts, and repressed material that is accompanied by an emotional response producing a state of relief in the patient is called
questions.explanation: In psychoanalysis, catharsis is the bringing to consciousness of repressed ideas, accompanied by the expression of emotions, thereby relieving tension.

questions.question_text: A 34 year old man who has a significant conflict with his partner has the following thoughts in the unconscious and the conscious level. 'I hate him' (unconscious); 'I don't hate him' (conscious). This refers to which of the following defence mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Denial is the defence mechanism by means of which any aspect of reality, e.g. forbidden thoughts, is actively denied. With this defence mechanism, 'I hate him' becomes 'I don't hate him.' Note that this does not become 'I love him,' which would be reaction formation.

questions.question_text: A man with bilateral below knee amputation comes to vascular clinic but continues to talk about weather instead of his illness. The most likely defence mechanism employed is
questions.explanation: Denial is a refusal to accept external reality because it is too threatening—commonly used by people with severe physical illnesses. Seeing but refusing to acknowledge what one sees or hearing and negating what is heard are examples of denial. Denial avoids becoming aware of some painful aspect of reality.

questions.question_text: Which of the following ego defence mechanism has been put forth as an explanation for phobia?
questions.explanation: In psychoanalysis, displacement is a defense mechanism involving redirection of emotions from their original object to a substitute one by a chain of associations. The substitute object may be less threatening than the original one, and the displacement may therefore have the effect of avoiding or reducing anxiety. Freud invoked the mechanism of displacement to explain the fear of horses in Little Hans. The fear of his father was displaced on to horses.

questions.question_text: A patient involuntarily admitted in a psychiatric ward always shouts at the new cleaner on the ward, but does not show his anger towards the doctor or social worker who committed him to the hospital. The most likely defence mechanism employed here is
questions.explanation: In psychoanalysis, displacement is a defense mechanism involving redirection of emotions from their original object to a substitute one by a chain of associations. The substitute object may be less threatening than the original one, and the displacement may therefore have the effect of avoiding or reducing anxiety.

questions.question_text: Nomifensine is an antidepressant that has noradrenaline, dopamine and also serotonin reuptake inhibition properties. It has been withdrawn due to its propensity to cause which of the following side effects?
questions.explanation: Nomifensine has noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin reuptake inhibition properties. It was withdrawn due to haemolytic anaemia in a small number of patients. It was a particularly effective antidepressant for patients with epilepsy as it did not alter the seizure threshold. In 1986 the product licences for nomifensine were voluntarily surrendered by its manufacturers and the drug was withdrawn worldwide. Haemolytic anaemia was the most frequently reported serious reaction with nomifensine, although other adverse effects also caused concern (thrombocytopaenia, hepatotoxicity, allergic alveolitis, and febrile illness).

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications is preferred option to treat a 75 year old man with a relapse of psychotic depression and has been taking treatment for prostatic hypertrophy in addition to high cholesterol?
questions.explanation: High-potency neuroleptics, such as haloperidol have lower anticholinergic effects and are less likely to cause urinary retention compared to low-potency medications such as chlorpromazine in elderly patients with prostatic hypertrophy. Clozapine is not recommended because of its powerful anticholinergic effects, its tendency to cause hypotension, and the risk for agranulocytosis. Thioridazine can cause fatal arrhythmias by prolonging the QT interval, in addition to the high anticholinergic profile. Finally, olanzapine may not be appropriate due to cholesterol related issues.

questions.question_text: A bipolar disorder patient on lithium treatment developed signs of severe lithium toxicity. What is the best immediate treatment option?
questions.explanation: Moderate and severe lithium toxicity require aggressive approaches. Initial general antipoisoning measures like gastric lavage may be helpful, but ultimate success depends upon elimination of lithium from the body. Haemodialysis will rapidly eliminate lithium from the body.

questions.question_text: Tardive dyskinesia induced by psychotropics is attributed to which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: One theory explaining tardive dyskinesia (TD) is that nigrostriatal D2 receptors most sensitive to blockade trigger a form of undesirable neuroplasticity called super-sensitivity in reaction to D2 receptor blockade. If D2 receptor blockade is removed early enough, TD may reverse. This reversal is theoretically due to a 'resetting' of super-sensitive D2 receptors by an appropriate return to normal in the number or sensitivity of D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway once the antipsychotic drug that has been blocking these receptors is removed. However, after long-term treatment, sometimes the D2 receptors apparently cannot reset back to normal, even when D2 blocking drugs are discontinued. This leads to TD that is irreversible, persisting whether or not D2 blockers are administered.

questions.question_text: A 67-year-old gentleman has been on treatment for depression. He went to the local beach for sunbathing on a summer day afternoon and presented to A and E complaining of nausea, dizziness and leg cramps. Which electrolyte disturbance is most likely?
questions.explanation: Most antidepressants are strongly linked with hyponatraemia. The clinical features of hyponatraemia include nausea, dizziness, lethargy, confusion, cramps and seizures. Other risk factors in this case include old age, warm weather and drug treatments such as diuretics.

questions.question_text: A 65 year old woman who is being treated for depression comes to the Medical Emergency Unit with lethargy, cramps, poor memory and weight loss on a hot afternoon. She is taking some unknown psychotropic medication for a long time. Also, more recently, she started taking 'water tablets' for swelling in her legs. Which of the following is a likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: The story is suggestive of hyponatraemia induced by diuretics and antidepressants. Most antidepressants have been associated with hyponatraemia. Signs of hyponatraemia include dizziness, nausea, lethargy, confusion, cramps, and seizures. Risk factors include: older age, female gender, major surgery, history of hyponatraemia or a low baseline sodium concentration, co-therapy with other drugs known to be associated hyponatraemia (e.g. diuretics, NSAIDs, antipsychotics, carbamazepine, cancer chemotherapy, calcium antagonists, ACE inhibitors, and laxatives), reduced renal function, medical comorbidity, and low body weight.

questions.question_text: What is the most serious risk involved in treating a patient with combination of clozapine and carbamazepine?
questions.explanation: Clozapine can cause neutropenia/agranulocytosis. Carbamazepine commonly causes a chronic low white blood cell count. One patient in 20,000 taking carbamazepine develops agranulocytosis and/or aplastic anaemia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following agents is most likely to have caused a newborn to have a defect of the tricuspid valve?
questions.explanation: Valproate induced neural tube effects are predominantly lumbosacral, but anencephaly is also seen occasionally. Tricuspid defects may be seen in lithium-treated patients, with extreme cases having full-blown Ebstein's anomaly. There may be an increased risk of Ebstein's anomaly if lithium is taken during the first trimester, though the size of risk is uncertain. More recent data suggest the magnitude of effect is much smaller than previously estimated. Recent data has shown an association with maternal mental health problems generally rather than specifically with lithium.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following drug usage has been associated with hyperparathyroidism?
questions.explanation: Hypocalcaemia and hyperparathyroidism are uncommon side effects associated with lithium therapy. Lithium increases the risk of hyperparathyroidism, and some recommend that calcium levels should be monitored in patients on long-term treatment.

questions.question_text: A depressed patient experiences constipation and dry mouth whilst on amitriptyline. This is mainly due to
questions.explanation: Amitriptyline and other tricyclic antidepressants can induce anticholinergic side effects such as constipation, dry mouth and urinary retention. Muscarinic receptor blockade leads to anticholinergic side effects, especially through M3 receptor blockade.

questions.question_text: Which of the following agents exert an allosteric action on the nicotinic receptors?
questions.explanation: Galantamine has an allosteric action on nicotinic receptors, producing a stimulating or alerting effect, similar to the effect of nicotine use.

questions.question_text: Antipsychotic drug induced akathisia is due to;

options.text: Dopamine D2 receptor activation in the hippocampus
Low dopamine D2 receptor occupancy in striatum
High dopamine D2 receptor occupancy in striatum

correct_answer.text: High dopamine D2 receptor occupancy in striatum

correct_answers.text: High dopamine D2 receptor occupancy in striatum

questions.explanation: Antipsychotic drug-induced akathisia is thought to be due to high dopamine D2 receptor occupancy in the striatum. Higher doses of antipsychotic medications are correlated with higher D2 receptor occupancy and worse subjective experience of akathisia. Most extrapyramidal symptoms are related to D2 receptor occupancy and, in particular, akathisia has an important subjective component. The exact aetiology of akathisia is unknown, but it is thought to be due to antipsychotic agents blocking D2 receptors in the brain. The general belief is that there is an imbalance between cholinergic/dopaminergic or serotonergic/dopaminergic systems. The location where this imbalance occurs is most likely the shell of the nucleus accumbens.

questions.question_text: A patient with depression is being treated by antidepressant medications. Which of the following changes may be observed?

options.text: Increasing expression of corticosteroid receptors in the brain

correct_answer.text: Increasing expression of corticosteroid receptors in the brain

correct_answers.text: Increasing expression of corticosteroid receptors in the brain

questions.explanation: Antidepressants reduce HPA axis activity by increasing negative feedback from steroid hormone. This is made possible via increased corticosteroid receptors.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most likely mode of action of disulfiram?
questions.explanation: Disulfiram causes irreversible inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase, resulting in the accumulation of acetaldehyde. This leads to signs and symptoms such as flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, tachycardia and palpitations if alcohol is consumed.

questions.question_text: Which symptom is acknowledged as part of cocaine withdrawal?
questions.explanation: Rapid cessation of euphoric effects occurs due to the rapid metabolism of cocaine, resulting in withdrawal effects that can lead to repeated use. A characteristic feature of cocaine withdrawal is intense cravings for cocaine with a striking lack of many physical withdrawal symptoms. Other signs/symptoms include dysphoria, anhedonia, anxiety, tremulousness, lethargy, fatigue, nightmares, headache, profuse sweating, muscle cramps, stomach cramps, and insatiable hunger.

questions.question_text: With respect to the neurotransmitter glutamate, which of the following is true?

options.text: It is synthesized by the enzyme glutamate decarboxylase

questions.explanation: Glutamate is the major excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system. NMDA, AMPA, and kainite receptors for glutamate are all members of the ligand-gated ion-channel family of receptors. These ligand-gated ion channels are also known as ionotropic receptors. GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter, produced from glutamate via glutamic acid decarboxylase.

questions.question_text: Xanomeline has been advocated as a novel approach to treat schizophrenia. It acts via
questions.explanation: Xanomeline, as an M4/M1 central agonist, decreases dopamine cell firing in the ventral tegmental area. This would theoretically reduce positive psychotic symptoms. Xanomeline also increases extracellular levels of dopamine in the prefrontal cortex, which theoretically would improve cognitive, negative, and affective symptoms. Combined with tropsium, it has shown promising efficacy and tolerability for the psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Tom is on clozapine for treatment resistant psychosis. He is embarrassed about hypersalivation and wet-pillows every morning. The most likely mechanism of this adverse event is

options.text: M4 receptor agonism and alpha 2 receptor antagonism
M4 receptor agonism and alpha 1 receptor antagonism
M4 receptor antagonism and alpha 2 receptor antagonism
M4 receptor antagonism and alpha 2 receptor antagonism
M4 receptor antagonism and alpha 1 receptor antagonism

correct_answer.text: M4 receptor agonism and alpha 2 receptor antagonism

correct_answers.text: M4 receptor agonism and alpha 2 receptor antagonism

questions.explanation: The pharmacological basis of clozapine-related hypersalivation remains unclear. Suggested mechanisms include muscarinic M4 agonism, adrenergic alpha-2 antagonism, and inhibition of the swallowing reflex.

questions.question_text: Which antidepressant is a presynaptic alpha-2 antagonist and now classified as NaSSA?
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine is a dual serotonin and norepinephrine agent. It is an alpha-2 antagonist and NaSSA (noradrenaline and specific serotonergic agent).

questions.question_text: Which one among the following has very limited potential for causing a hypertensive crisis?
questions.explanation: Moclobemide is a reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase A. It has a much reduced risk of interactions with tyramine than non-selective MAOIs. At higher doses, foods with high tyramine should still be avoided.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered to be the therapeutic blood level of clozapine?
questions.explanation: Routine blood level monitoring with clozapine is not recommended. However, increasing the dose until a plasma level of 350 ng/mL is achieved is sometimes recommended.

questions.question_text: Which of the following follows zero order kinetics?
questions.explanation: Most clinically relevant drugs tend to follow first-order pharmacokinetics. In contrast, a few drugs follow zero-order elimination in which the drug amount decreases by a constant amount over time regardless of the initial concentration (i.e., ethanol).

questions.question_text: Which of the following antipsychotics is primarily renally excreted?
questions.explanation: Amisulpride and sulpiride are primarily renally excreted. Both are best avoided in the setting of renal failure.

questions.question_text: A 23 year old patient is observed to consume high amounts of coffee whilst in the ward. She is being treated for a depressive episode. Which of the following statement is likely to be true in this case?

options.text: Caffeine reduces renal clearance of lithium
Caffeine can interact with drugs that are metabolised by CYP1A2

correct_answer.text: Caffeine can interact with drugs that are metabolised by CYP1A2

correct_answers.text: Caffeine can interact with drugs that are metabolised by CYP1A2

questions.explanation: Caffeine is metabolised by CYP1A2, a hepatic cytochrome enzyme that exhibits genetic polymorphism, which may partially account for the large inter-individual differences that are seen in the ability to tolerate caffeine. CYP1A2 is induced by smoking and inhibited by several drugs such as fluvoxamine (which may decrease caffeine clearance by 80% and precipitate caffeine toxicity). Caffeine competitively inhibits CYP1A2, so plasma levels of some drugs may be reduced if caffeine is withdrawn. Controlling caffeine intake when investigating renal function using lithium clearance is important as caffeine has a natriuretic effect and increases lithium clearance as well.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs when combined with lithium do NOT cause an increase in lithium levels per se but still cause increased incidence of neurotoxicity?
questions.explanation: Haloperidol and clozapine can produce increased neurotoxic effects with lithium without altering the plasma levels.

questions.question_text: Performance sub-sets of WAIS-R include all but
questions.explanation: Verbal subtests include similarities, arithmetic, digit span, vocabulary, information and comprehension tests. Performance subtests include picture arrangement, block design, picture completion, digit symbol, matrix reasoning. Digit span is a verbal subtest.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following tests measures non-verbal IQ?
questions.explanation: WAIS has both verbal and performance tests. Verbal tests include similarities, arithmetic, digit span, vocabulary, information and comprehension. Performance tests include picture arrangement, block design, picture completion, digit symbol and matrix reasoning. Digit Symbol is a performance subtest measuring non-verbal IQ.

questions.question_text: Patients with Gerstmann syndrome usually demonstrate which of the following?
questions.explanation: Gerstmann syndrome is characterised by left-right disorientation, agraphia, acalculia, and finger agnosia, generally associated with lesions in the parietal lobe of the dominant cerebral hemisphere.

questions.question_text: Epileptic automatisms usually last for
questions.explanation: Epileptic automatism is a state of clouding of consciousness which occurs during or immediately after a seizure. Simple stereotyped behaviours such as gesturing, grasping, lip-smacking and chewing movements often last few seconds to minutes.

questions.question_text: The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) assesses which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test is a widely used test of abstract thinking, planning, and ability to alter mental set as circumstances require. It is regarded as a good indicator of frontal lobe damage and is especially useful for identifying perseveration.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old lady has been diagnosed with normal pressure hydrocephalus. Which of the following symptoms is more likely to improve following shunting?
questions.explanation: Several studies have found that compared with other symptoms, gait disturbance shows better and sustained improvement following shunting in normal pressure hydrocephalus.

questions.question_text: Raven's progressive matrices is used to assess
questions.explanation: The Raven's Progressive Matrices is a non-verbal test that is widely used to assess general cognitive ability. Each item shows a geometric pattern with a missing piece, and participants must select the correct option that completes the pattern.

questions.question_text: In a psychological test, the clinician reads an incomplete sentence 'The captain wanted to stay with the sinking?' and asks the patient to complete the sentence. Which of the following test is being carried out?
questions.explanation: Failures in semantic inhibition are frequently measured with the Hayling Sentence Completion test. In the Hayling test, the individual is presented with 30 sentences where the last word is missing and must either complete them with the obvious word or, in the inhibition section, with an unrelated word.

questions.question_text: Lesions of the dominant parietal lobe may produce Gerstmann syndrome. Which of the following is not a feature of this syndrome?
questions.explanation: Gerstmann syndrome is characterised by left-right disorientation, agraphia, acalculia, and finger agnosia. Hemi-neglect is not part of this tetrad.

questions.question_text: Which of the following movement disorders is characterized by involuntary flinging movements of the extremities?
questions.explanation: Lesions in the subthalamic nucleus yield ballistic movements, sudden limb jerks of such velocity that they are compared to projectile movement. Hemiballismus is a rare movement disorder causing involuntary flailing, ballistic movements of the limbs.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old gentleman suffers from anterograde memory loss with preserved insight. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anterograde amnesia is most frequently seen in patients who have sustained injuries to the medial temporal lobes or the diencephalon. Damage to the hippocampal formation causes severe anterograde amnesia.

questions.question_text: Many medical conditions are associated with autistic behavioural phenotype. Which one of the following is NOT associated with autism?
questions.explanation: The cause of autism is unknown, but genetic associations exist (e.g. Down syndrome, fragile X), obstetric complications, toxic agents, maternal infections, autoimmune factors, and associations with neurological disorders such as tuberous sclerosis and neurofibromatosis. Huntington's disease is not linked to an autistic phenotype.

questions.question_text: The negative symptoms of schizophrenia are related to which of the following neurobiological phenomena?
questions.explanation: Positive symptoms of schizophrenia have been associated with excessive dopamine transmission in subcortical regions, whereas negative symptoms are related to a concomitant deficit in cortical dopamine transmission. fMRI studies have shown reduced activation during prefrontal cognitive tasks in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in nonmedicated patients.

questions.question_text: A man is unable to mimic the action of hammering a nail as instructed by the examiner. He is exhibiting:
questions.explanation: Ideomotor apraxia is characterised by the impaired ability to imitate unfamiliar actions. It is also called motor apraxia or ideokinetic apraxia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following tests of WAIS is resistant to brain damage?
questions.explanation: The WAIS hold tests are vocabulary, information, object assembly and picture completion. Information is considered a hold test resistant to brain damage.

questions.question_text: If a 34 year old mother suffers from schizophrenia, what is the lifetime morbid risk for her only child for schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Genetic factors account for most of the liability to schizophrenia. The risk of developing schizophrenia when one has an affected parent is approximately 12–15%.

questions.question_text: Mrs. X has adopted a child from family of alcohol dependent parents. The risk of her adopted child suffering from alcohol dependence is increased by
questions.explanation: Close relatives of those with alcohol use disorders have a 3–4 times increased risk for severe alcohol problems. Children of alcoholics have increased risk of development of alcohol problems themselves, even when adopted into families without alcohol problems.

questions.question_text: The odds of having panic disorder is increased in first degree relatives of patients with panic disorder compared to general population by a factor of
questions.explanation: Several family studies have documented an increased panic disorder risk among affected individuals' relatives. Among relatives, the prevalence varies between 6 to 17%, which translates to an average of 4–8 times increase in the risk.

questions.question_text: A 24 year old woman suffers from bipolar affective disorder. The risk of her twin brother developing bipolar affective disorder is
questions.explanation: The risk in dizygotic twins is 5–15%. ('Dizygotic' as it is a twin brother. Twin sister could have been either monozygotic or dizygotic.)

questions.question_text: Patients with Down's syndrome have higher risk of Alzheimer's disease. Which of the following gene is implicated in this relationship?
questions.explanation: Several genes that might play a role in the development of Alzheimer's are found in chromosome 21, including the amyloid precursor protein. Overexpression of the APP gene may be related to the overproduction of A-beta peptide in senile plaques.

questions.question_text: The isoforms A and B of enzyme Monoamine oxidase are encoded on chromosomes
questions.explanation: Both isoforms of MAO are encoded on chromosome X.

questions.question_text: In Alzheimer's which of the following is true

options.text: Decreased acetylcholine with increased glutamate levels
Increased acetylcholine with increased glutamate levels

correct_answer.text: Decreased acetylcholine with increased glutamate levels

correct_answers.text: Decreased acetylcholine with increased glutamate levels

questions.explanation: The cholinergic hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease is predicated on the observation that cognitive deterioration results from progressive loss of cholinergic neurons and decreasing levels of acetylcholine in the brain. Glutamate has been hypothesised to be released in excess in Alzheimer's, leading to excitotoxicity.

questions.question_text: Sigma receptors are associated with
questions.explanation: Selective sigma-1 receptor agonists have been shown to produce antidepressant-like effects in animal models, suggesting a role in depression.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old gentleman has moderate level of learning disability with expressive language disorder, social anxiety, impulsivity, marked inattention. Molecular genetic testing may show an expansion of which repeats?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is caused by an expansion of CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene. Full mutation (>200 repeats) leads to gene silencing and intellectual disability. Premutation carriers (55–200 repeats) may have other clinical features.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common side effect of a phosphodiesterase (type 5) inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, such as sildenafil, are used to treat erectile dysfunction. Common side effects include headache, flushing, nasal congestion, dyspepsia and muscle aches due to vasodilatory effects on capillaries.

questions.question_text: Sally is being treated for a major depressive episode with Phenelzine for the last few months. Her GP calls you to inform you that she has been diagnosed with a medical disorder and asks if she should continue the antidepressant. You advise that she should stop the antidepressant. Which illness from the list below is most likely to have prompted this advice?
questions.explanation: The use of non-specific MAOIs like phenelzine is contraindicated in patients with phaeochromocytoma or other tumors of the adrenal medulla that secrete pressor substances. MAOIs inhibit the breakdown of pressor amines, leading to hypertensive crises.

questions.question_text: The presence of 2 or more cell lines from different zygotes in a single individual is called
questions.explanation: A chimera is an organism composed of cells derived from two or more distinct zygotes. In contrast, mosaic organisms have different cell lineages originating from the same zygote.
